items.stem: Explain the causes of urban air pollution in LIC and NIC cities.
items.answer: Rapid growth in vehicle numbers with old engines and poor fuel; industry and power stations burning coal; domestic burning of wood, charcoal and waste; construction dust; weak regulation; inversions and basin sites trap pollutants.

items.stem: Explain the difference between point and non-point source pollution and why the latter is harder to control.
items.answer: Point sources come from one identifiable outlet; non-point sources are diffuse (run-off from farms and roads), so they are hard to monitor, regulate and treat.

items.stem: Kenji argues that economic development inevitably leads to environmental pollution. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to Kuznets curve, industrialisation and technology.
items.answer: For: Industrialisation and urbanisation in China, India and earlier in the UK caused severe air and water pollution; consumption and waste rise with income. Against: The environmental Kuznets curve suggests pollution falls at higher incomes with regulation and cleaner technology (London, Los Angeles, Beijing since 2013); policy can decouple growth from pollution. Conclusion: Pollution often rises in early development, but it is not inevitable: policy and technology can reduce it.

items.stem: Explain the causes of environmental degradation.
items.answer: Population growth and rising consumption; industrialisation and urbanisation; poverty forcing overuse of resources; weak regulation and enforcement; market failure where pollution is not priced; inappropriate technology.

items.stem: Explain the consequences of water pollution for ecosystems.
items.answer: Oxygen depletion from organic waste kills fish; eutrophication causes algal blooms and dead zones; toxins and heavy metals bioaccumulate in food chains; loss of biodiversity.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that poverty is the main cause of environmental degradation? In your answer you may refer to governance and ecological footprint.
items.answer: For: The poor depend directly on natural resources and may overuse land, forests and fuelwood; they lack capital for conservation. Against: Consumption in wealthy countries, industrial pollution, TNC activity, commercial agriculture and weak governance cause far greater total degradation; ecological footprints are highest in HICs. Conclusion: Poverty contributes locally, but wealth, consumption and industrial activity are the larger causes globally.

items.stem: Explain how environmental degradation affects human health.
items.answer: Air pollution causes respiratory and heart disease; contaminated water spreads cholera and diarrhoea; toxins (mercury, lead, arsenic) cause poisoning and birth defects; degraded land reduces nutrition.

items.stem: Explain how environmental degradation affects livelihoods.
items.answer: Declining fish stocks, soil erosion and salinisation reduce incomes; tourism falls; ill health reduces ability to work; costs of treatment; forced migration.

items.answer: Deaths are modelled from exposure-response relationships, not counted; monitoring stations are few; other causes of disease such as smoking overlap.

items.stem: Diego argues that the health effects of environmental degradation are more serious than its effects on livelihoods. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to fisheries and poverty.
items.answer: For: Millions of premature deaths a year from air pollution and unsafe water; long-term poisoning (Minamata, arsenic in Bangladesh). Against: Loss of livelihoods (fisheries, soils, tourism) affects far more people, deepening poverty, which itself harms health; the two are closely linked. Conclusion: Health and livelihood effects reinforce each other; health effects are the most direct, but livelihood loss is more widespread.

items.answer: Not correct. Flint, Michigan (lead in water, 2014) and air pollution in European cities show HICs are affected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Household air pollution from cooking fires is a major health risk in LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Toxins can become more concentrated at higher levels of food chains.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Burning wood, charcoal and dung indoors causes respiratory disease, especially among women and children. (b) Correct. This biomagnification affected people eating fish at Minamata.

items.stem: Table 21.3 shows the estimated number of premature deaths attributed to air pollution in one year in four cities, with their populations: City A: 15 223 deaths, population 18.4 million; City B: 2 831 deaths, population 2.7 million; City C: 28 124 deaths, population 25.8 million; City D: 3 866 deaths, population 2.7 million. Suggest why these estimates are uncertain.
items.answer: Deaths are modelled from exposure-response relationships, not counted; monitoring stations are few; other causes of disease such as smoking overlap.

items.stem: Table 21.3 shows the estimated number of premature deaths attributed to air pollution in one year in four cities, with their populations: City A: 23 786 deaths, population 15.9 million; City B: 11 471 deaths, population 16.1 million; City C: 8 464 deaths, population 29.8 million; City D: 15 016 deaths, population 29.7 million. (a) Explain why rates are a better basis for comparison than total deaths. (b) Suggest why these estimates are uncertain.
items.answer: (a) Cities have very different populations, so totals reflect size; rates show the risk to an individual. (b) Deaths are modelled from exposure-response relationships, not counted; monitoring stations are few; other causes of disease such as smoking overlap.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the health effects of environmental degradation are more serious than its effects on livelihoods?
items.answer: For: Millions of premature deaths a year from air pollution and unsafe water; long-term poisoning (Minamata, arsenic in Bangladesh). Against: Loss of livelihoods (fisheries, soils, tourism) affects far more people, deepening poverty, which itself harms health; the two are closely linked. Conclusion: Health and livelihood effects reinforce each other; health effects are the most direct, but livelihood loss is more widespread.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that economic development inevitably leads to environmental pollution. In your answer you may refer to industrialisation and technology.
items.answer: For: Industrialisation and urbanisation in China, India and earlier in the UK caused severe air and water pollution; consumption and waste rise with income. Against: The environmental Kuznets curve suggests pollution falls at higher incomes with regulation and cleaner technology (London, Los Angeles, Beijing since 2013); policy can decouple growth from pollution. Conclusion: Pollution often rises in early development, but it is not inevitable: policy and technology can reduce it.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the tragedy of the commons. (b) A student writes: “Environmental degradation affects only the environment, not the economy.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Each user of a common resource gains the full benefit of extra use but shares the cost of degradation with others, so without regulation the resource is overused and degraded. (b) Not correct. It reduces fisheries, farm yields, tourism and health, costing economies heavily.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the tragedy of the commons. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Poverty can be both a cause and a consequence of environmental degradation.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Each user of a common resource gains the full benefit of extra use but shares the cost of degradation with others, so without regulation the resource is overused and degraded. (b) Correct. The poor may overuse resources and also suffer most from degradation.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.answer: (a) 4.2 mg/l; 47.7% (b) Organic waste raises BOD, so bacteria decomposing it use up oxygen faster than it is replaced, reaching a minimum at about 5 km; downstream, as the waste is broken down and the water is re-aerated by turbulence and photosynthesis, oxygen recovers.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “waterborne disease”?
options: The means by which people secure the necessities of life, such as farming, fishing or wage labour.
An illness caused by micro-organisms in contaminated water, such as cholera and typhoid.
Discarded electronic equipment, often processed informally in LICs, releasing lead, mercury and dioxins.
The build-up of toxins such as mercury or pesticides in organisms over time and up food chains.
items.answer: An illness caused by micro-organisms in contaminated water, such as cholera and typhoid.
